summary: For every future Artemis Kid… Experience a true-to-life lunar simulation powered by real NASA data. Step into the boots of a junior astronaut and dive into an interactive story in this 3D Moon-base adventure game for kids aged 7–12! As the mission's very first crew member, your goal is to build humanity's first home on the Moon—so your family and friends can one day join you. Guided and encouraged by Professor Luna, every choice you make shapes your journey! This adventure pulls you into the deep mysteries of space, where you’ll face thrilling, high-stakes challenges. Will you pack your supply rocket with food, or bring a new crew member? You can't choose both—from rocket launches to daily survival, every choice demands a tough decision! Experiment with different strategies, overcome unexpected challenges, and collect fascinating Fact Cards packed with real space science. Through replayable adventures and tough trade-offs, kids discover the real challenges humanity faces when building and sustaining a home beyond Earth!
details:
Artemis Kids — Project Solution

Artemis Kids is a free, browser-based 3D lunar base simulation game for children aged 7–12. Stepping into the role of junior astronauts at the Moon’s south pole, players explore realistic terrain, construct a sustainable outpost, and manage interconnected life-support resources—electricity, oxygen, water, food, communication, and radiation shielding.

Rather than memorizing space facts, children learn scientific and engineering principles firsthand through exploration, trade-offs, and problem-solving.

How It Works

Gameplay follows a continuous learning cycle alternating between two phases:

Active Phase (Explore, Build & Decide) → Rest Phase (Review, Resupply & Plan) → Next Active Phase

  • Active Phase — Explore and Build: Players navigate a 3D lunar landscape and build habitats, solar panels, batteries, communication antennas, greenhouses, and life-support systems. Because lunar terrain and sunlight affect facility performance, placement matters. Systems are tightly linked: life support requires water and electricity to produce oxygen, while greenhouses need resources and crew members to grow food. Outdoor activities also require managing spacesuit oxygen, radiation exposure, and equipment maintenance.
  • Active Phase — Respond to Unexpected Hazards: Space-weather alerts introduce simplified radiation hazards during outdoor tasks, forcing players to choose between continuing their mission or retreating to shelter.
  • Rest Phase — Review and Prepare: After returning to the habitat, players receive a Mission Control report summarizing base status, resource levels, and potential risks. Using rule-based diagnostics and clear explanations, players identify bottlenecks and plan priorities for the next Active Phase.
  • Rest Phase — Plan Supplies from Earth: During the Rest Phase, players can order supplies from Earth within strict rocket cargo limits. They must balance immediate survival needs, such as food, against long-term growth requirements, including construction materials, spare parts, and additional crew members. Deliveries take time to arrive, making advance planning essential.
  • Talk With Professor Luna — Your Own Mission, Not Someone Else’s: At key moments the story pauses and players answer Professor Luna by choosing a reply. For example, they can say “Nice to meet you!” or “I’m a little nervous…” after landing, or “I miss my family” when they first see Earth rising over the lunar horizon. Players only choose; they never type. The screen dims so the choice stands out, and the professor responds to the player’s own words. At the end of training, he recalls how the player felt at the start. This conversation turns the tutorial from watching a simulation into living the mission as the first crew member, so children experience the Moon base as their own story rather than from a third-person view.
  • Learn Science Through Play: A scientist guide named Professor Luna leads an approximately 30-step tutorial supported by visual markers, a glossary, Japanese furigana, and English text.
    In addition to explanations, Professor Luna can now talk directly with the player through short interactive conversations. Players respond by choosing from simple dialogue options, allowing them to reflect on what they see and connect scientific ideas with their own feelings and decisions.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Artemis Kids aims to help young learners develop practical STEM skills through interactive decision-making:

  • Systems Thinking & Cause-and-Effect: Understanding how power, water, oxygen, food, and crew size affect one another as an interconnected system.
  • Resource & Risk Management: Making trade-offs under cargo, oxygen, and environmental constraints while prioritizing crew safety during space-weather events.
  • Accessible, Transparent Science: Combining Japanese/English support, furigana, and touch controls with a dedicated in-game data view that distinguishes real NASA data from simplified gameplay models.
  • Ownership & Engagement: Through dialogue choices, children speak as the astronaut themselves. They don’t just watch a character, and this sense of ownership keeps young players motivated through a long, system-heavy simulation.

Our Goal & Future Vision

Our goal is to turn NASA data into an interactive experience where children learn by making decisions and seeing their consequences.

While formal classroom effectiveness studies remain future work, we plan to expand Artemis Kids with additional lunar landing sites, historical space-weather scenarios, classroom activity modules, and a Mars mission mode.

Bringing NASA Data to the Next Generation of Space Explorers.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Frontend & 3D Engine: TypeScript, Babylon.js, Vite, pnpm
  • Testing, Quality & Hosting: Vitest, Biome, Cloudflare Pages
  • Architecture & Accessibility: Modular simulation engine (separating environmental calculations, resource logic, 3D rendering, and UI feedback), bilingual support (Japanese with furigana / English), and browser-local progress storage.

About the NASA Data Field

We entered as many of the NASA open data sources and resources we used as the project form's "NASA Data" field allows, but we reached its entry limit.

The complete list is available inside the game: open the pause menu and select the "Data" tab ("Where the data comes from").

It shows every data source we used, including the NASA DONKI space-weather events, the LOLA lunar terrain (NASA PGDA), the NASA photos and the Blue Marble Earth image, and every real-world value used in the simulation with a link to its source.

Play Artemis Kids: https://nasa-spaceapp.pages.dev/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/LunaInsidious/NASA-SpaceApp
